tagline: An old trading passage carries a highway and transcontinental freight.
intro: The Abo Pass Trail follows NM 47 and US 60 through a mountain passage between the Manzano Mountains to the north and the Los Pinos Mountains to the south. Designated a New Mexico Scenic and Historic Byway in 1998, it connects Belen with the remnants of Abo Pueblo. The New Mexico Tourism Department presents that connection as its central story: east-west trade that began on foot and continues by train. US 60 and the BNSF railroad both use Abo Pass, whose elevation is 5,771 feet.

Salt, beans, cotton and buffalo meat traveled over the pass before the highway existed. Spanish travelers later used the passage between the Rio Grande valley and their three salt missions northeast of the pass. Later, the Santa Fe railroad sought a gentler alternative to Raton and Glorieta passes; its Belen Cutoff opened in 1908 and quickly carried the bulk of its transcontinental freight. The Atlantic and Pacific Highway followed through the pass in 1921, becoming US 60 in 1931.

From Rio Communities, take NM 47 south to US 60, then follow the highway east through Abo Pass. On the eastern side, Abo Pueblo occupies ground near springs; the separate community of Abo lies on US 60 amid low mesas and red-sandstone stream cuts.

moments.title: Abo Canyon
moments.text: The railroad’s advantage here was a matter of gradient. The Santa Fe’s older route crossed Raton and Glorieta passes on grades reaching 3.5 percent; the Abo Canyon alternative held to no more than 1.25 percent. Completed in 1908, the Belen Cutoff soon took most of the company’s transcontinental freight. Passenger service through the canyon ended in 1971 with the cancellation of the San Francisco Chief. Freight continued on what became BNSF’s Southern Transcon, but the canyon remained a four-mile single-track bottleneck until a second track was completed in March 2011.

moments.title: Abo Pueblo
moments.text: Abo Pueblo occupied ground near a cluster of springs on the eastern slope of the pass. Its Tompiro-speaking Tanoan community farmed at high elevation, with little surface water for irrigation and sparse rainfall. Salt deposits and access to the bison herds of the Great Plains helped make these settlements viable. The Tompiros traded salt, bison skins and meat between Plains peoples and the Rio Grande pueblos. Spanish missionary work began here in 1622, followed by church construction in 1629. The pueblo and mission ruins are preserved within Salinas Pueblo Missions National Monument.

moments.title: Abo
moments.text: Red sandstone forms low mesas and stream cuts near Abo, the US 60 community distinct from the nearby pueblo and mission ruins. A railroad arrived in 1912, and Abo grew into a small town with a school before its abandonment by 1940. In 1933, more than 200 men failed to find a fugitive hiding in the arroyos and badlands around Abo. The community’s railroad-era history is separate from the much older pueblo nearby, which formed part of an earlier trade route.
